titleText.es: Si no eres lo bastante guay para hacerlo a mano, puedes mirar herramientas como Upside-Down-Ternet para jugar con la gente de tu wifi.
titleText.en: If you're not cool enough to do it manually, you can look up tools like Upside-Down-Ternet for playing games with people on your wifi.
titleText.noteEn: Upside-Down-Ternet is the name of a network-prank tool alluded to by the original comic's title text.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you must be; I suppose you are (a guess about now)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Estarás has the form normally used for future 'you will be,' but Spanish can also use a future-shaped verb to make a tentative guess about the present. The context and questioning tone select that conjecture meaning.

example.en: You must be tired, I suppose?

cardDefinitions.noteEn: With a network or connection, Spanish con can describe the service someone is using. Natural English may use 'on' instead of the usual literal translation 'with.'

example.es: Trabajo con la red de la oficina.
example.en: I work using the office network.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Wifi is used as a Spanish noun. It is often feminine because red, 'network,' is understood: la wifi. Usage and pronunciation vary by region.

example.es: La wifi del hotel es lenta.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Admin is an informal shortened form of administrador or administradora, especially common in computing and online communities.

example.es: Ella es la admin del servidor.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: appeals to; is someone's thing (in irle la marcha)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In irle la marcha a alguien, va does not describe physical movement. The fixed expression says that excitement or action appeals to that person.

example.es: A Leo le va la aventura.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In the expression irle la marcha a alguien, la marcha means excitement, energetic action, or even a taste for trouble rather than a literal march.

example.es: A Sara le va la marcha.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I will put; I will set up
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Pondré is the future form of poner for yo, 'I.' Poner changes its stem to pondr- before the future ending -é. With me and an item, context can suggest putting it on or getting oneself set up with it.

example.en: Tomorrow I will install a new lock.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Used on its own as an exclamation, vaya can express surprise, admiration, or annoyance. This conversational use is distinct from vaya as a form of the verb ir, 'to go.'

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; part of caerse when an online service, connection, or network goes down
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With an online service, connection, or network, caerse means to go down or drop. Se stays before the changed form of caer: el servicio se cae for one service and las conexiones se caen for several connections.

example.es: La conexión se cae a menudo.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Caen is the present form of caer for more than one thing. With se and network services, it describes connections failing or going down rather than objects literally falling.

example.es: A veces las llamadas se caen.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en cuanto, 'as soon as'
no separate English word; completes en cuanto, 'as soon as'
to send; to pass (data through something)
tunnel; protected route for network traffic
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In networking, a tunnel carries one kind of traffic inside another connection, often to link a device securely to a remote network.

example.es: Los datos pasan por un túnel cifrado.
example.en: The data passes through an encrypted tunnel.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Deja is the positive command for tú from dejar. In dejar de followed by an action verb, it tells one person to stop that action rather than to leave something behind.
Intentar is the verb's unchanged dictionary form, meaning 'to try.' Lo is attached to its end and stands for the thing or action being tried.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: holy shit; damn (vulgar exclamation in Spain)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hostia has a religious literal origin, but as an exclamation in Spain it commonly expresses shock or alarm. It can sound vulgar or offensive, so it is unsuitable in formal settings.
Insertando is insertar's ongoing-action form ending in -ando. It can follow a form of estar to describe an action in progress.
Solicito is the present form of solicitar for yo, 'I.' Although it resembles English 'solicit,' its ordinary Spanish meaning is simply to request or apply for something.

example.en: I request a copy of the report.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Editando is editar's ongoing-action form ending in -ando. A preceding form of estar may be understood from a nearby coordinated action.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en vivo, 'live' or 'in real time'
live; in real time (in en vivo)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Vivo usually means 'alive,' but the fixed expression en vivo describes something transmitted, performed, or handled as it happens.

example.en: We listen to the program live.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cielos literally means 'skies' or 'heavens.' Used alone as an exclamation, it expresses surprise or concern and is generally mild.

example.en: Good heavens, it is very late!

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to have ... you (helper haber with te attached)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Haber is the unchanged helper used before a completed-action form. Te is attached to its end and marks informal singular 'you' as the person affected by the later action.
Avisado is avisar's completed-action form, also called a past participle. It stays unchanged after the helper haber.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: pwned; thoroughly beaten or hacked (internet slang)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Pwneado is a playful Spanish adaptation of the English internet slang pwned. The borrowed stem is treated like a Spanish verb and given the completed-action ending -eado; after han, it describes the completed defeat or compromise. It is informal and nonstandard.

example.es: Nos han pwneado en la partida.
example.en: They pwned us in the match.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Besides meaning 'well,' bien can strengthen a description or completed result. Its natural English equivalent may be 'really,' 'thoroughly,' or another emphatic wording.

example.en: The door ended up firmly closed.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Sentar is the verb's unchanged dictionary form. Te is attached to it to form sentarte, which focuses on the listener taking a seated position.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone likes excitement, energetic action, or a bit of trouble?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching short person word with ir, followed by la marcha; you can put the word a before the person to name who enjoys it.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person: me va la marcha means that I like excitement, while le va la marcha says that he, she, or formal 'you' does. La marcha is singular, so the usual verb form is va. To identify the person explicitly, put the word a before that person, as in a Marta le va la marcha.

example.es: A Marta le va la marcha.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you reassure someone that something is not a problem?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Say no hay problema, meaning 'no problem' or 'that's fine.'
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is a common conversational reassurance. Hay is the unchanged form meaning 'there is' or 'there are'; Spanish normally uses problema without an article in this fixed response.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: caerse un servicio, una conexión o una red
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that an online service, connection, or network goes down?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of caerse with the service, connection, or network that becomes unavailable.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Caerse is caer with a matching short word such as se. The verb changes to match the number of things: el servicio se cae for one, but las conexiones se caen for more than one. In this technical use, nothing literally falls.

example.es: La conexión se cae cada noche.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: en cuanto, seguido de una acción habitual
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that one repeated or habitual action happens as soon as another one does?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use en cuanto before the ordinary present form of the action that sets the time.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: En cuanto works as one time connector meaning 'as soon as.' For a repeated or habitual fact, the following verb uses an ordinary present form. For one awaited future event, Spanish normally uses a special form instead: en cuanto llegue means 'as soon as I arrive,' with llegue rather than llega.

example.es: El perro ladra en cuanto oye un ruido.
example.en: The dog barks as soon as it hears a noise.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is happening live, in real time?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use en vivo after the activity, event, or medium.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: En vivo is a fixed adverb-like expression. Vivo stays in this form even when the noun is feminine or plural; the phrase describes the activity as it happens rather than describing something as biologically alive.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone is able to do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of ser, then capaz de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The dictionary form, also called the infinitive, is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Ser changes for the person and time, and capaz becomes capaces for more than one person. Keep de before the final action verb, which remains unchanged.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: ataque de intermediario en una red
cardDefinitions.answerEn: an attacker secretly intercepts traffic between two endpoints and may block or alter it before forwarding it
cardDefinitions.noteEn: VPN and SSH encryption are designed to resist this kind of interference. The joke exaggerates Mrs. Roberts's skill: she detects new tunnels immediately, disrupts connections, and even changes requested pages and the live TCP data stream.

Por stands alone in this brief conversational follow-up because the usual qué in por qué is understood from context.

applications.explanationEn: Conexiones is plural, so the network-failure expression uses se caen rather than singular se cae.
En cuanto introduces the immediate time relationship, and intento begins the present-time action that triggers it.
Intento changes for the speaker, while pasar remains in its unchanged dictionary form and algo fills that action's object slot.

applications.explanationEn: Qué carries an accent because it adds an exclamatory degree before the following description.
Deja changes into a command, de is the required link, and intentarlo keeps the action verb in its dictionary form with lo attached.
Deja is dejar's positive command form for one person addressed informally.
Lo is attached to the unchanged verb intentar and stands for the thing being tried.

applications.explanationEn: Está supplies the helper for one person, and insertando supplies the ongoing action with its -ando ending.
En vivo marks the data-stream editing as occurring in real time rather than after the fact.

regions.labelEs: NADIE ES TAN RÁPIDO. ¿QUIÉN ES EL ADMIN?

applications.explanationEn: Quién carries an accent because it directly asks for a person's identity.

regions.labelEs: CIELOS. GRANUJAS DEL VECINDARIO EN LA RED INALÁMBRICA.
DEBERÍA HABERTE AVISADO SOBRE LA SEÑORA ROBERTS.

excludedUnits.rationale: Roberts is a person's English-language surname, not a Spanish lexical word target.

applications.explanationEn: Debería supplies the retrospective judgment, haberte combines the helper haber with te, and avisado is avisar's completed-action form.
Te is attached to the dictionary form haber and marks the listener as the person affected by the later action.

regions.labelEs: ¿CÓMO ES CAPAZ DE TECLEAR CON MANOPLAS?

applications.explanationEn: Cómo carries an accent because it directly asks about the manner in which something is possible.
Es matches one person, capaz de introduces the ability, and teclear stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the action.

regions.labelEs: TÍO, TE HAN PWNEADO BIEN. QUIZÁ DEBERÍAS SENTARTE.

applications.explanationEn: Han is the present helper for an unnamed plural actor, and pwneado is the borrowed verb's completed-action form.
Deberías gives advice to one informal listener, and sentarte keeps the action verb in its dictionary form with te attached.
Te is attached to the dictionary form sentar to focus the action on the informal listener taking a seat.
